name: Superior saber-cut and acromial approaches
corridor: Either a front-to-back saber cut over the AC joint to the posterior acromion, or a superior deltoid split from the mid greater tuberosity across the anterior acromial tip toward the spine, with optional partial deltoid/trapezius release

positioning.text: Position so the AC joint, acromion, greater tuberosity, and scapular spine can be palpated.

surface_landmarks.text: For the saber cut mark the AC joint and the dorsal acromial rim. For the superior deltoid split mark the acromion, greater tuberosity, and scapular spine.

incision.text: Saber cut: start anteriorly over the humeral head, cross the AC joint, and end at the posterior acromion; it can join a deltopectoral cut in front or a posterior approach behind. Superior split: start at the midpoint of the greater tuberosity and aim at the spine, crossing just posterior to the anterior acromial tip.

superficial_interval.text: The superior split goes through the acromial part of deltoid in line with its fibers and can be extended into a standard deltoid split.

deep_interval.text: Partially detach deltoid and trapezius if needed to see the full acromial fracture line. If the split is carried inferiorly, the axillary nerve crosses about 6 cm distal to the lateral acromion.

layers.text: Skin, deltoid/trapezius origin, then the AC joint and acromion.

structures_at_risk.text: The axillary nerve if a superior split is extended inferiorly, and the deltoid/trapezius origins if they are released and not repaired.

danger_zones.text: A distal deltoid-split extension more than about 5–6 cm below the acromion is the axillary-nerve danger zone.

retraction_hazards.text: Release muscle only as far as the fracture requires so it can be reattached.

exposure.text: The saber cut shows the AC joint and acromion. The superior split shows simple acromion fractures and can be used for proximal-humeral nailing.

limitations.text: Neither window exposes the scapular body. Distal deltoid-split length is capped by the axillary nerve.

indications.text: Used to expose the AC joint and acromion, including simple acromion fractures, periprosthetic acromial fractures around reverse or anatomic prostheses, and as a superior extension for proximal-humeral nailing.

closure.text: Reattach released muscle and close fascia, fat, and skin in layers.

complications.text: Complications include axillary-nerve injury from an over-long inferior split and failure to reattach deltoid or trapezius.

procedure_applications.condition: An acromion or AC-joint fracture is exposed from superior, with optional extension into a deltoid split or deltopectoral interval
A periprosthetic acromial fracture around a reverse or anatomic prosthesis is exposed from superior

questions.question: Where does a saber-cut incision run?
questions.answer: From over the humeral head, across the AC joint, to the posterior acromion.

questions.question: Where does the superior acromial split start and aim?
questions.answer: From the midpoint of the greater tuberosity toward the scapular spine, crossing just posterior to the anterior acromial tip.

questions.question: How far below the acromion does the axillary nerve typically cross?
questions.answer: About 6 cm distal to the lateral acromial border.
